groups.title: API Design Principles
groups.question: Your Next.js app exposes an API to partners, uses a paid AI API key and receives payment webhooks. Explain how you would design and secure these endpoints.

followUps.REST conventions for route handler desig: How would you apply REST conventions to your route handlers?
followUps.Securing API keys and secrets on the ser: Where can a secret API key safely be used in a Next.js app?

evidence.text: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH updates and DELETE removes.
URLs name resources, like /api/posts/42.
Following conventions makes the API predictable for other developers.
Keys are only used in server components, server actions or route handlers.
Anything in client components ends up in the browser bundle.
Keys come from server-side environment variables without a public prefix.
Services like Stripe sign each webhook request.
Verifying the signature proves the request really came from them.
Without it, attackers could send fake events, such as fake payments.

groups.title: External Integrations Theory
groups.question: You are adding payments and profile photo uploads to your app. Explain how payment intents work and how you would handle large file uploads.

followUps.Stripe payment intents and checkout flow: How is a payment split between the server and the browser?
followUps.File upload strategies and storage optio: Why upload files directly to storage with a pre-signed URL?

evidence.text: A payment intent represents one payment attempt and tracks its status.
The server creates it with the amount.
The browser confirms it with the card details, which go straight to Stripe.
The browser uploads straight to object storage like S3 or R2.
A pre-signed URL gives temporary permission for that one upload.
Large files never pass through your server, which saves time and resources.

notEnough: Only saying you upload to S3.

groups.title: Stripe Integration
groups.question: You are adding checkout to your Next.js store and must record orders even if the customer closes the browser. Explain the Stripe flow.

followUps.Stripe Checkout and payment link setup: How does Stripe Checkout work from a server action?
followUps.Handling Stripe webhooks in a route hand: How should the webhook route handler process payment events?

evidence.text: A server action creates a Checkout Session with the items.
The user is redirected to Stripe's hosted payment page.
Stripe handles card validation and extra verification like 3D Secure.

notEnough: Only saying you redirect to Stripe.

evidence.text: It verifies the Stripe signature using the raw request body.
It updates the order in the database for events like completed checkout.
It handles the same event arriving twice without double-processing.

groups.title: Environment Config and External APIs
groups.question: Production crashed because an environment variable was missing, external API calls open new connections every time, and a public endpoint is being abused. Explain how you would fix each.

followUps.Typed environment variables with Zod val: Why validate environment variables with Zod at startup?
followUps.Calling third-party APIs securely from s: How should server code call third-party APIs?
followUps.Rate limiting and CORS for public route: How would you protect a public route handler from abuse?

evidence.text: The environment is parsed against a schema when the app starts.
Missing or malformed values fail immediately with a clear error.
The rest of the code gets typed, trusted config.

notEnough: Only saying you validate env vars.

evidence.text: Calls happen in server components or actions so keys stay private.
A shared SDK client is reused instead of created per request.
Errors and timeouts are handled so one slow API does not hang the page.

notEnough: Only saying you call APIs from the server.

evidence.text: Rate limits cap how often a client can call it.
Limits use a shared store, like Redis, since serverless instances do not share memory.
CORS headers restrict which browser origins may call it.

notEnough: Only saying you add rate limiting.
